products.overview: Capture spatial and spectral information from your sample in a single hyperspectral microscope.
features: 400–1620 nm Hyperspectral Coverage: IMA™ hyperspectral microscopy across VIS, NIR and SWIR wavelengths from 400–1620 nm.
Spatial & Spectral Imaging: Acquire spatial and spectral information together for microscopic material and sample analysis.
Millions of Data Points in One Snapshot: High-throughput IMA™ hyperspectral imaging for millions of spatial and spectral data points in a single snapshot.
Patented Imaging Filter Technology: Photon etc. patented imaging filter technology for rapid hyperspectral data acquisition.
Brightfield Hyperspectral Microscopy: IMA™ brightfield hyperspectral microscopy for spatial and spectral analysis of microscopic samples.
Darkfield Hyperspectral Microscopy: IMA™ darkfield hyperspectral microscopy for transparent, low-contrast and optically challenging samples.
Multiple Measurement Modes: Photoluminescence, electroluminescence, fluorescence, reflectance and transmittance imaging in one hyperspectral platform.
Scientific-Grade VIS, NIR & SWIR Microscopy: Configurable scientific-grade microscopy across VIS, NIR and SWIR spectral regions for advanced materials research.

applications: Advanced Materials Analysis: Hyperspectral characterization of complex materials — Photon etc. identifies solar cells, nanomaterials and semiconductor quality control as key advanced materials applications for IMA™.

Solar Cell Research: PL and EL mapping of photovoltaic materials — supports hyperspectral characterization of photovoltaic materials and devices, with spatial information showing where a response occurs and spectral information providing additional detail about the emission.

Nanomaterial Research: Spatial and spectral characterization of nanomaterials — relevant where nanomaterials exhibit optical properties that vary with composition, structure, size, or local environment.

Semiconductor Quality Control: Hyperspectral PL/EL analysis — useful when the optical or electroluminescent response of a semiconductor needs to be mapped across a device or sample for non-destructive characterization.
Infrared Marker Research: SWIR hyperspectral microscopy — supports studying infrared markers in complex environments, including tissues and living cells.

Transparent Material Imaging: Darkfield hyperspectral microscopy — suited to transparent and low-contrast samples such as polymers, crystals and living cells, where conventional brightfield contrast may not provide sufficient information.
Polymer Research: Spectral imaging of transparent polymers.
Crystal Characterization: Hyperspectral imaging of crystals.

Perovskite Research: Photoluminescence mapping — demonstrated by Photon etc. for photoluminescence mapping of perovskite crystals under intense excitation, using monochromatic images and spectra collected from selected regions of the crystal.
Living Cell Research: Hyperspectral SWIR imaging of suitable samples.

faqs.question: What is IMA™?
faqs.answer: IMA™ is a hyperspectral microscope from Photon etc. that captures spatial and spectral information across the 400–1620 nm range.

faqs.question: What is IMA™ used for?
faqs.answer: IMA™ is used for hyperspectral characterization of advanced materials, solar cells, nanomaterials, semiconductors, infrared markers, transparent materials, crystals, polymers and other research samples.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does IMA™ cover?
faqs.answer: IMA™ provides hyperspectral coverage from 400 to 1620 nm, spanning the VIS, NIR and SWIR regions.

faqs.question: What does IMA™ measure?
faqs.answer: IMA™ can rapidly map photoluminescence, electroluminescence, fluorescence, reflectance and transmittance.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure photoluminescence?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ supports photoluminescence mapping and Photon etc. demonstrates the system for PL mapping of perovskite crystals.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure electroluminescence?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ can map electroluminescence and is positioned for applications including solar-cell and semiconductor research.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ perform fluorescence imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ supports hyperspectral fluorescence imaging.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure reflectance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Reflectance is one of the measurement modes supported by IMA™.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ measure transmittance?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ supports transmittance measurements for suitable samples.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ be configured as a darkfield microscope?
faqs.answer: Yes. IMA™ can be configured as either a brightfield or darkfield hyperspectral microscope.

faqs.question: What samples can be studied using darkfield IMA™?
faqs.answer: Photon etc. identifies transparent materials such as polymers, crystals and living cells as applications for hyperspectral darkfield microscopy.

faqs.question: How many data points can IMA™ acquire?
faqs.answer: Photon etc. states that IMA™ can acquire millions of data points in a single snapshot.

faqs.question: How is IMA™ different from point-by-point hyperspectral scanning?
faqs.answer: IMA™ uses high-throughput imaging filters for rapid hyperspectral acquisition, rather than relying on standard point-by-point scanning.

faqs.question: What type of microscope does IMA™ use?
faqs.answer: IMA™ combines a scientific-grade VIS, NIR and/or SWIR microscope with Photon etc.'s patented imaging filter technology.

faqs.question: Is IMA™ suitable for solar-cell research?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. identifies solar-cell research as an application and highlights PL and EL hyperspectral analysis.

faqs.question: Is IMA™ suitable for nanomaterial research?
faqs.answer: Yes. Advanced materials and nanomaterial analysis are listed among IMA™ applications.

faqs.question: Is IMA™ suitable for semiconductor analysis?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. identifies semiconductor quality control using hyperspectral PL and EL as an IMA™ application.

faqs.question: Can IMA™ be used for infrared marker research?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. identifies research involving infrared markers in complex environments, including tissues and living cells, using hyperspectral SWIR microscopy.

longForm.heroLead: Capture spatial and spectral information from your sample in a single hyperspectral microscope. Photon etc. IMA™ is a hyperspectral microscope designed to acquire spatial and spectral information across the 400–1620 nm range. By combining a scientific-grade VIS, NIR and/or SWIR microscope with Photon etc.'s patented imaging filter technology, IMA™ enables detailed spectral characterization of a wide range of materials. IMA™ can acquire millions of data points in a single snapshot and rapidly map photoluminescence (PL), electroluminescence (EL), fluorescence, reflectance and transmittance. The system can be configured as either a brightfield or darkfield hyperspectral microscope, making it suitable for different sample types and imaging requirements. Unlike point-by-point scanning approaches, IMA™ uses high-throughput imaging filters to acquire hyperspectral information rapidly across the sample. IMA™ is suited to applications including advanced materials analysis, solar cell and nanomaterial research, semiconductor quality control, infrared marker studies, and hyperspectral imaging of transparent materials.

sections.title: How IMA™ Works
body: Traditional microscopy provides detailed spatial information about a sample; hyperspectral microscopy adds spectral information to those spatial features, and IMA™ combines the two.
The workflow: Sample → Microscopic imaging → Hyperspectral acquisition → Spatial + spectral data → Material characterization.

Each measured region can therefore be considered in terms of both where a feature is located and what its spectral response is — this is particularly useful when visually similar regions need to be distinguished by their optical or spectral properties.

Compared with conventional microscopy, IMA™ acquires spectral information within the same hyperspectral imaging workflow rather than requiring a separate measurement, uses high-throughput imaging acquisition rather than point measurements, and provides spectral information across 400–1620 nm rather than a limited spectral context.
